chapter.title: What counts as a good argument

cards.body: As far as anyone knows, Socrates wrote nothing, and Athens put him on trial and to death after a lifetime of asking awkward questions. Western philosophy is one dinner-table argument that has run for about 2,500 years, and he was the guest who kept turning to whoever had just spoken and asking *why*. An opinion is only a seat at that table. **A claim plus the reasons that hold it up is an argument**, and that is what earns you a hearing.
cards.simpler: As far as anyone knows, Socrates never wrote anything down. The city of Athens put him on trial and to death after a lifetime of asking awkward questions. Western philosophy is like one long dinner-table argument that has lasted about 2,500 years. Socrates was the guest who kept asking whoever had just spoken why they believed it. Having an opinion only gets you a seat at that table. **A claim plus the reasons that hold it up is an argument**, and that is what earns you a hearing.

cards.prompt: At dinner your cousin Dev says: 'Pineapple on pizza is a crime. I've hated it since I was 6.' Which part is the claim, the thing he wants you to accept?

options.text: Both sentences are claims; there is no reason here

whyNot.b: That's the reason, not the claim: it's the fact Dev holds up to back the verdict, not the verdict itself.
whyNot.c: That's two sentences, not two claims: the second one has a job, trying to hold the first one up. Whether it manages is a separate question.

cards.reteach: The claim is the sentence someone wants you to walk away believing. The reason is whatever they point at when you say 'why?'. Dev wants you to believe pineapple pizza is a crime, and his 6-year-old self is the evidence he offers.

cards.title: Two parts, every time
cards.body:
Every opinion worth arguing about has two parts. The *claim* is the sentence someone wants you to agree with. The *reasons* are what they say when you ask why.

You'd think the hard part is finding the reasons. It isn't. People hand you reasons all day, on buses, in group chats, across tables. The hard part is noticing **whether the reasons are actually touching the claim**, or just sitting next to it on the plate.

Try it on the next advert you see. Underline the claim. Circle what's offered as 'because'. Often there is nothing to circle.
cards.simpler: Every opinion has two parts. The claim is the sentence someone wants you to agree with. The reasons are what they say when you ask why. Finding reasons is easy. People give them all day, on buses and in group chats. The hard part is noticing **whether the reasons actually touch the claim** or sit next to it. Try this with the next advert you see. Underline the claim. Circle the because. Often there is nothing to circle.

cards.title: Priya and the 12%
cards.body: Priya's landlord emails: 'Rent goes up 12% in March. Everyone's rent is going up.' The claim is that her rent should rise 12%. The reason is that everyone's is rising. She writes back one line: 'Whose rent, and by how much?' Two days of silence, then a reply offering 8%. **The reason was true and still didn't carry the number.**
cards.simpler: Priya's landlord sends an email. Rent goes up 12% in March, it says, because everyone's rent is going up. The claim is that her rent should rise 12%. The reason is that everyone's rent is rising. She writes back one line: whose rent, and by how much? Two days of silence. Then a reply offering 8%. **The reason was true and still did not carry the number.**

cards.prompt: A friend says: 'This phone is the best one you can buy. It's the one I have.' Does her reason hold up her claim?

options.text: Yes: owning it means she knows it's good
No: the reason tells you what she bought, not whether it's the best
Yes, as long as she's happy with it

whyNot.a: That's familiarity, not support: knowing one phone well tells you about that phone, not how it ranks against the ones she has never used.
whyNot.c: That's a different claim: 'I'm happy with mine' would be held up by her being happy. 'Best you can buy' needs a comparison, and none was offered.

cards.reteach: Ask one question: if the reason is completely true, does the claim follow, or at least become likely? She really does own that phone. 'Best you can buy' still isn't supported, because 'best' is a comparison and she compared it with nothing.

cards.title: The test: grant it, then ask
cards.body:
Here is the one test. **Grant the reason completely**, pretend it is 100% true, then ask: does the claim now have to be true, or at least become much more likely? If yes, the reason holds. If the claim is left as open as before, the reason is decoration.

This is why a reason can be true and still useless. 'Everyone's rent is rising' was true. It makes some rise likely, but 'therefore 12%' did not follow. Picture the reason as a bolt. A solid bolt fitted to the wrong door keeps nothing shut.

So a good argument is not one with true-sounding reasons. It is one where the reasons, once granted, leave the claim little room to hide.
cards.simpler: Here is the one test. **Grant the reason completely**, as if it were fully true, then ask whether the claim now has to be true, or at least becomes much more likely. If yes, the reason holds. If the claim is left as open as before, the reason is only decoration. 'Everyone's rent is rising' was true. It makes some rise likely, but 'so 12%' did not follow. A strong bolt on the wrong door keeps nothing shut. Good reasons, once granted, leave the claim little room to hide.

cards.body: Priya nearly signed. 'Everyone's rent is rising' was true, and **a true reason feels like support**. That feeling is the trap. Spot it this way: the moment a reason checks out, grant it, then ask whether the 12% follows from it. Some rise, maybe. That exact number, not yet.
cards.simpler: Priya almost agreed to the 12%. 'Everyone's rent is rising' was true, and **a true reason feels like support**. That feeling is the trap. It is like a key that is real but belongs to a different lock. Here is how to spot it: the moment a reason checks out, grant it, then ask whether the 12% follows from it. Some rise, maybe. That exact number, not yet.

cards.prompt: Which of these is a complete argument: a claim with a reason that, if granted, holds it up?

options.text: 'We have to leave by 7 to catch the start. The film starts at 7:30 and the drive takes 30 minutes.'
'We have to leave by 7. I just feel it.'
'We have to leave by 7. Last time we were late you blamed me.'

whyNot.b: That's a claim with a mood, not a reason: a feeling tells you about the speaker, not about when the film starts.
whyNot.c: That's a grievance, not a reason: who got blamed last time has no bearing on tonight's start time.

cards.reteach: Run the test. Grant that the film really starts at 7:30, the drive really takes 30 minutes, and the goal is to catch the start, and leaving by 7 follows. Grant the feeling, grant the old blame, and 7 still floats free, unsupported.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: Every opinion is a claim plus reasons, and the key test is this: **if the reasons were fully true, would the claim have to follow, or at least be likely?** Many arguments fail that test with reasons that are perfectly true and beside the point: a solid bolt fitted to the wrong door.
cards.simpler: Every opinion is a claim plus reasons. The key test is this: **if the reasons were fully true, would the claim have to follow, or at least be likely?** Many arguments fail that test. Their reasons are perfectly true and still beside the point, like a strong bolt on the wrong door that keeps nothing shut.

cards.body:
Open your last group chat where someone had an opinion. Find the claim. Find the 'because'. Grant the 'because' fully and ask whether the claim follows. Reply with nothing. Just notice.

Tomorrow: the reply that never touches your claim, and why it so often wins the room anyway.
cards.simpler: Open the last group chat where someone shared an opinion. Find the claim, the thing they wanted everyone to agree with. Find the because, the reason they gave. Now **grant the because fully and ask whether the claim follows**. Do not reply. Do not correct anyone. Just notice what you see, the way you might notice a loose button without sewing it on. Tomorrow: the reply that never touches your claim, and why it so often wins the room anyway.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now split any opinion into its claim and its reasons, and say whether the reasons hold it up.

dubious_claims: 'None of Socrates' writing survives' suggests he wrote things that were lost. As far as anyone knows he wrote nothing, apart from a mention in Plato's Phaedo that he put Aesop's fables into verse in prison. 'He wrote nothing' is the accurate line.

'The only test that matters: if the reasons were fully true, would the claim have to follow?' This is the test for logical proof only (called deductive validity). It wrongly rules out strong evidence-based arguments, where true reasons make the claim likely but not certain. 'Everyone's rent is rising' is a fair reason for some rise.
The answer to exercise 3, option a, doesn't fully pass the chapter's own must-follow test. It only works if you assume they want to arrive on time and nothing goes wrong, like traffic or parking.
repairedFrom.why: The Marco card teaches a second idea, the reply that attacks the person instead of the claim. It never uses the chapter's grant-the-reason test, and it gives away what the closing line promises for tomorrow.
repairedFrom.fix: Swap Marco for a mistake that uses this chapter's test: Priya almost accepts the 12% because 'everyone's rent is rising' is true. The tell is that a true reason feels like support. Grant it and ask whether the 12% has to follow. Save the reply-about-the-person for tomorrow.
